sections.h2: Does North Carolina have its own capital gains tax on a house sale?
sections.html:
No. The Department of Revenue's rate page lists one flat individual rate and no separate rate for gains. North Carolina taxes the gain through its flat individual income tax, using the federal figure as the starting point and then applying state adjustments.

G.S. 105-153.5, titled "Modifications to adjusted gross income," lists what a taxpayer may deduct from, or must add to, adjusted gross income to reach North Carolina taxable income. Nothing in that section creates a different rate for gains on a home, so a gain that remains taxable after the federal rules lands in the same income calculation as wages.

sections.h2: What is the North Carolina income tax rate for 2026?
sections.html:
The Department of Revenue prints 3.99% for taxable years after 2025, and 4.25% for taxable years beginning in 2025. The same page says additional rate changes may apply starting with 2027, depending on rate reduction triggers in Session Law 2023-134.

sections.h2: How does the federal home sale exclusion affect a North Carolina seller?
sections.html:
The IRS lets you exclude up to $250,000 of gain on your main home, or up to $500,000 on a joint return. Because North Carolina begins with federal adjusted gross income, gain the IRS excludes does not usually reach your state return either.

To qualify, the IRS says you must meet the ownership test and the use test:

  • You owned the home for at least 24 months of the 5 years before the sale.
  • You used it as your residence for at least 24 months of that 5-year period.
  • On a joint return, either spouse may meet the ownership test, but both must meet the use test.
  • You generally cannot have excluded gain from another home during the two years before this sale.

The two years need not be continuous, and they may fall in different periods within the five. Military and certain foreign service members may suspend the five-year period for up to 10 years if they qualify as being on official extended duty. IRS Publication 523 holds the full rules and worksheets.

sections.h2: When must a North Carolina seller report the sale?
sections.html:
You report it on the federal return if you receive a Form 1099-S, even when the entire gain is excludable, and also if you cannot exclude all of the gain. The IRS points to Schedule D and Form 8949 for that reporting.

North Carolina then asks for a state return when gross income passes the filing threshold for your status. NCDOR prints these tax year 2025 figures for federal gross income:

  • Single: a return is required if gross income exceeds $12,750.
  • Married filing jointly: $25,500.
  • Head of household: $19,125.
  • Qualifying surviving spouse: $25,500.

An installment sale, where part of the price is paid in a later year, is reported under the installment method unless you elect out, and the home sale exclusion remains available even then. A seller who moved during the year may be a part-year resident, and nonresidents with income tied to North Carolina real property also file Form D-400 with Schedule PN, which apportions income to the state.

sections.h2: What federal capital gains rates apply if the gain is taxable?
sections.html:
For taxable years beginning in 2025, the IRS says the rate on most net capital gain is no higher than 15% for most individuals. A gain you held for more than one year is long-term, while a gain on property held one year or less is taxed as ordinary income.

The IRS lists the thresholds for tax year 2025 this way:

  • 0% applies if taxable income is at or below $48,350 for single filers, $96,700 for joint filers and $64,750 for heads of household.
  • 15% applies above those amounts up to $533,400 for single, $600,050 for joint and $566,700 for head of household.
  • 20% applies to the extent income exceeds the 15% ceiling.
  • Unrecaptured section 1250 gain, which is the portion tied to depreciation on real property, is taxed at a maximum of 25%.

The IRS also notes that high earners may owe the net investment income tax, and that a taxable gain can create a need for estimated tax payments. Losses on a personal home are not deductible.

sections.h2: How do inherited and rental houses change the picture?
sections.html:
A house you inherited has its own basis rules, and the IRS refers owners to Publication 551 for assets received by gift or inheritance. The IRS also says holding period exceptions apply to property acquired from a decedent, which is why heirs should read Publication 544 before assuming the one-year line.

North Carolina repealed its estate tax. G.S. 105-32.1 through 105-32.8 were repealed by Session Laws 2013-316, effective January 1, 2013, for decedents dying on or after that date. A house that passes through an estate is therefore taxed at the state level only through the income tax when it is later sold.

A rental house has to pass the same use test as any other home, meaning you lived in it as a residence for 24 of the last 60 months. The IRS lists a 25% maximum rate on unrecaptured section 1250 gain from real property, so a seller of a tenant-occupied house should ask a CPA to review the figures before signing a contract.

sections.h2: Which North Carolina adjustments matter when you sell?
sections.html:
A few items in G.S. 105-153.5 show up in real estate planning. They are state adjustments to federal income, and they decide how much of the federal figure North Carolina taxes.

  • Standard deduction: $12,750 for single and married filing separately, $19,125 for head of household and $25,500 for married filing jointly or a surviving spouse.
  • Itemized deduction for mortgage interest on a qualified residence plus real estate taxes: capped at $20,000 combined, and the cap applies to both spouses together.
  • Medical and dental expenses and charitable gifts are among the other itemized items.
  • Gain that federal law defers into a qualified Opportunity Fund must be added back for North Carolina purposes, with a matching deduction later to prevent double tax.
  • Basis differences: if North Carolina basis in a property differs from federal basis, an adjustment applies in the year you sell it.

From 2014 through 2025, North Carolina also required an addition for mortgage debt discharged on a principal residence, even though federal law excluded it. That matters to a seller who completed a short sale or a loan forgiveness in those years.

sections.h2: Is the deed excise tax part of capital gains tax?
sections.html:
No. The excise tax is a transfer fee that the seller pays to the register of deeds before the deed is recorded, at $1.00 on each $500.00 of value or fractional part. It does not reduce or replace the income tax.

Still, keep it with your records. The IRS defines a capital gain as the amount realized from the sale minus your adjusted basis, and it says basis is generally the owner's cost. Keep the closing statement, the original purchase documents and receipts for improvements together so your preparer can work out both numbers.

faqs.q: Does North Carolina tax capital gains on the sale of a home?
faqs.a: Yes, through its income tax. North Carolina uses a flat rate of 3.99% for taxable years after 2025, applied to income that begins with the federal figure, with no separate rate for home sale gains.

faqs.q: Can I exclude gain on my North Carolina house from federal tax?
faqs.a: Often yes, up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 on a joint return, if you owned and lived in the home for at least 24 months of the last 5 years. You generally cannot have used the exclusion on another home within two years.

faqs.q: Do I have to report a house sale if the gain is excluded?
faqs.a: Yes, if you receive a Form 1099-S. The IRS says the sale must be reported even when the whole gain is excludable.

faqs.q: What is the North Carolina income tax rate for 2025?
faqs.a: It is 4.25% for taxable years beginning in 2025, according to the Department of Revenue. The rate for taxable years after 2025 is 3.99%.

faqs.q: Does North Carolina have an estate tax on a house I inherit?
faqs.a: No. The estate tax statutes were repealed for decedents dying on or after January 1, 2013. An heir who later sells the house may still owe income tax on a gain.
